A further objection says that God's will to create the world must be either eternal or new. If it is eternal, it either remains after the world has passed away, in which case it seems to will an existing thing at a time when it does not exist, or it relates only to the world's past existence, which makes no sense. If the will disappears, then something eternal has vanished. If the will is new, it must be caused by another will, leading to an endless chain. And if God changes from one state to another, He would be a body, made of parts and powers, as those claim who imagine Him as a subject in which successive intentions arise.

This and similar objections come from comparing God's will to ours and imagining it as a decision or resolve to create. They also assume that things that occur in time are present to God only after being absent, or exist for Him only after not existing. This is not so. From eternity, God knows the whole chain of existence and the complete order, the relations among its parts, its beginning and end, and every stage in between. He knows that this precise order should come from Him and be realized in the world. This eternal knowledge, one with His essence, is His will to bring into existence all that has come into being and to send the light of existence to every thing. It brings them all out of nonexistence and hiddenness into existence and open appearance. This knowledge and will are one eternal reality. They do not change or pass from one state to another, either in themselves or in their relation to what they bring about.

Another objection says that God's will makes the action necessary; otherwise, the action would not happen. Once the will is directed toward it, the action cannot fail. So the world must follow from God's essence as heat follows fire or light follows the sun, and God would be a cause that acts by necessity rather than by choice. His will would be only a name, not a real attribute.

We answer, as we have repeatedly said, that God's essence is His will and approval. Will is truly the source from which action comes. This is the highest form of action through will. There is also a difference between what is necessary from God and what is imposed on God. God's essence is simple and is identical with His will, but it can also be considered in relation to the identities of possible things. Through His attributes and names, it bears relations to the distinct essences of things in His all-embracing knowledge, which is one and simple in one respect, yet detailed in another. Considered as existence, His essence has no composition of any kind—not in the mind, as in the analysis of broader kind and difference or essence and existence, and not in reality, as in the combination of matter and form. But when we consider the meanings of His attributes and names, the divine realm contains a great many relations. They do not divide God's oneness or simplicity.

When God's essence is considered together with these specific relations—which are called the “treasuries” of things, as in the verse “There is nothing whose treasures are not with Us”—He wills each kind of possible thing, and each individual in its number, time, and place. Each thing comes into being in its own time and place. If we consider God's essence without these specifying relations, no one created thing is distinguished from another, and no particular possible thing must follow. The action becomes necessary only when these relations are considered. So it is true that God brings things about through the specific ways His will relates to them, and each particular will is connected to a particular possible thing.

Some reports from our Imami leaders, preserved by the leading hadith scholars, say that will and “mashiyya” come into being and belong to God's acts, not to His essence. At first glance, this seems to conflict with our claim that His will is His essence. Our teacher and guide answers that “will” can mean the act of bringing things into being, the relation by which God creates them. It can also mean the created thing itself, which has come into being through that act.

Knowledge of created things has several levels. At its final level, those things exist outside the mind and are disclosed, not hidden, to God. In one respect, their own connected identities are His knowledge of them and what He knows; but His knowing them is not identical with their identities. His knowledge as the one who knows is His eternal essence. His knowledge as what is known is the created things themselves.

The same applies to will. At its final level, God's will is the actual existence of things. They are “will” in the sense that they are willed by Him, not in the sense that they are the act of His willing. The source of will, approval, and the power to specify things is God's own essence. This is a stronger account of choice than one in which God's will and approval arise from something added to Him. That is the substance of what our teacher says.

There is a great secret of divine knowledge that I will hint at here. A person with insight may see that the existence of things outside us belongs to God's knowledge and will—not only as what He knows and what He wills, but as the very act by which He knows and wills them. Anyone who understands the principles explained earlier can reach this insight.
Chapter 9 — Further support from reports of the Imams

As we explained earlier, when we want to do something or set out to obtain it, we first picture the action and judge that it will bring us some benefit. This judgment may be uncertain, imagined, or well founded. We may think the action will bring us a real good, or only an apparent one—something material, fame, praise, or honor that benefits our own being or one of our powers. From this thought and judgment, desire arises. When desire grows stronger, the power of will is stirred, and we resolve to act. In a human being, this will comes from a power higher than animal desire, which divides into appetite and anger: it comes from practical reason.

In other beings, the state of that power grows stronger in the way we have described. In both cases, will and desire set the powers in the muscles in motion. The muscles contract or extend, the nerves and limbs move, and the intended action takes place. In our outward actions, these starting points are separate. But God is far above multiplicity, outside motives, being acted upon, or taking delight in something beyond Himself. He is the end of every aim and desire. He has no desire, no love of anything other than Himself, and no purpose of obtaining something He lacks. Rather, He delights in Himself for His own sake. From this delight, all other good things and joys follow through His active giving and creation—not through being acted upon or acquiring something new.

Many Qur'anic verses point to this for those who reflect on them. God says, “God is self-sufficient, and you are the needy.” He is independent in every way of what is other than Him; everything else depends on Him in its essence, attributes, and actions. If His action and giving involved a separate purpose, desire, wish for obedience, or need for praise, He would not be fully independent of everything else. God also says, “To Him all things return,” and “To God all things come back.” These and many other verses show that He is the end of everything. His action has no end or purpose beyond His sacred essence. If He had a will added to His essence, or an outside motive that tipped Him toward action, He would not be the end of all things. These verses and others show that His will for things is identical with His knowledge of them, and both are His essence.

Reports from our Imami leaders, preserved in The Book of Knowledge and other hadith collections, include a sound report from Ṣafwān ibn Yaḥyā. He says: “I asked Abū al-Ḥasan to explain the difference between God's will and the will of created beings. He said: ‘A created being's will is an inner resolve, followed by the action that comes from it. God's will is His bringing things into being, and nothing else. He does not consider, worry, or think things over; these are the attributes of created beings. God's will is the act itself. He says to a thing, “Be,” and it is, without words, speech, resolve, thought, or any how—just as there is no how for Him.’”

By “inner resolve,” the report may mean that we picture an action, judge it beneficial, feel desire rise from our appetites, and then let that desire grow until we form a firm resolve called will. These are the stages of our deliberate actions. God is far above all of this. Our chosen actions pass through many states between our essence and what we do: some involve knowing, some deliberation, some appetite and anger, and some the bodily actions of pulling, pushing, attracting, or repelling. God's action, by contrast, follows directly from His essence. Nothing stands between Him and His action—not an added attribute or state, not an external motive, desire, intention, or any other change. His acts do, however, follow one another in an order, from the highest beings to those below them.

Hishām ibn al-Ḥakam relates a story about a skeptic who asked Imām al-Ṣādiq whether God feels approval and anger. The Imam answered: “Yes, but not as created beings do. Approval is a state that enters a created being and moves it from one state to another. A created being is ‘hollow’ and made up of parts; things enter into it. Nothing enters our Creator, for He is one, one in essence and one in meaning. His approval is His reward, and His anger is His punishment. Nothing enters Him to stir Him or move Him from one state to another, for that is the way of weak and needy creatures.” Al-Ṣadūq relates a similar report in The Book of Divine Unity: approval and anger are not states that enter God, for He is one in essence and meaning.

Calling a created being “hollow” is a striking and apt way to contrast it with God, who is al-Ṣamad—the One who needs nothing and to whom all turn. Every possible thing is made up of essence and existence. Essence by itself is like nothing; existence gives it form and definition, as though it surrounded an empty sphere and gave it boundaries. Every possible existence is also mixed with absences and shortcomings, so it has gaps corresponding to what it lacks. The farther existence moves from the source of good and generosity, the more lack and weakness it contains. It becomes, as it were, more hollow, thinner, and less substantial. Natural things are also composed of matter, which is what a thing may become, and form, which makes it actual. Form gives matter its identity, since matter by itself is indeterminate. In that sense, every material thing is hollow.

A thing is open to outside influences and passing states because it contains potential and possibility, along with absences or limitations. It therefore needs something to complete it—to bring it from absence to existence, from potential to actuality, from lack to fullness. God has placed in every created thing a movement toward the perfection and completeness suited to it, drawing it nearer to Him. For the beings nearest to God this takes the form of intellectual love; for higher souls, a longing of the soul; for lower souls, animal desire; and for natural things, change of position, size, quality, or place. Everything other than God has some lack or need and must be completed by something else. In this sense it is “hollow.” Only God is without any hollow or composition, whether from lack or from completion: He is the One, the Self-Sufficient.

Reports from our Imami leaders on this subject are numerous. I will cite only a few, so that the account does not become too long. Anyone who wants to read the rest can consult the hadith collections. Among other scholars who affirm God's oneness, Abū ʿAlī says in his notes on The Healing that all existing things come from God's essence and follow from it, so they do not oppose Him. Because He loves His own essence, all things that come from Him are willed for His sake. He does not will them for an aim beyond Himself, but because they follow from His essence. He does not will them simply for their own sake. If you love someone, you love the things that come from that person for that person's sake.

We will something because we desire or enjoy it, not because of the thing's own essence. If desire and pleasure could know themselves and produce their own actions, then they would will things for their own sake, since those things would come from them. But will belongs only to a being that is aware of itself.

The Necessary Being is complete—indeed, beyond complete—so He does not act for an aim outside Himself. He does not need to recognize something as good for Him, desire it, and then bring it about. His will is His knowledge that a thing is good in itself and must exist in a particular way to be truly good. No further will is needed to make it exist. His knowledge of the possible things arranged in the best order is itself the cause that brings them into being in that order. He does not first know what follows from His essence and then become pleased with it. Since these things come from what His essence requires, their coming from Him is itself His approval of them. Their existence does not conflict with Him; it fits His nature. Whatever comes from an agent in this way, and is known by that agent as its own act, is willed by it because it accords with its nature. So all things are willed by the Necessary Being, without His acting for a purpose beyond Himself.

This is like loving something for the sake of a person: the person is what you love in the fullest sense. The ultimate beloved is God Himself. We desire things because we need them, but the Necessary Being wills them in the way just described. He does not long for them, because He has no need of them. Purpose, in the sense of a motive for seeking something, involves desire: “Why did he seek it?” “Because he wanted it.” Where there is no desire, there is no such purpose. God has no aim in obtaining something or in the benefit that follows from obtaining it. An action itself can be an aim, or its benefit can be an aim: walking may be an aim, or exercise may be; building may be an aim, or the shelter it provides.

If someone understood the perfection that is the Necessary Being and then arranged everything below Him according to that model, so that all things were in the best order, the real aim would be the Necessary Being Himself, who is perfection. If He is both the source of action and its perfection, then He is both the agent and the end. The same is true if we build a house according to a perfection we have understood: that perfection is our aim. If the perfection itself were also the source of the building, then the source and aim would be one.

In us, a similar action may occur when we picture something and recognize it as useful or right. Unless some other factor favors a different course or blocks it, this thought moves our appetites. There is no further act of will between the thought and the appetite's movement; the thought itself is enough. God's will is similar: His understanding of things in the way described is the cause of their existence.

He does not need desire or a longing for what He does. We need desire and the power of longing so that we can use our limbs to obtain what suits us. Our limbs act only after desire. God needs no such desire or instruments. His knowledge of the whole order of existence, of the best way things should be, and of the best arrangement is providence itself. If we were to arrange existing things, we would first understand the best order, then arrange them according to it. When the order and perfection are the agent itself, and all things issue from that perfection, providence is present. It is God's will, and His will is His knowledge, because agent and aim are one.

Providence is God's understanding of how each thing should be: how a human being's parts must be arranged, or how the heavens must move, for each to be complete and for the good order to be present. This knowledge is not followed by desire or by a further purpose. God knows that what He knows accords with His own beloved essence. To say that He created the world for an aim below Himself—to make the world or the perfections that come with it His purpose—would mean seeking a perfection He would not have if He had not created the world. That does not befit the One who is necessary in every respect.

Avicenna concludes that God's will is His knowledge and providence, and is not something that comes into being. He also notes that when God conceives a thing, existence follows from that conception. When we conceive something, desire follows; when we desire it, our limbs move to obtain it. Power means that an action follows from will, with no added condition. In God, power is His knowledge: when He knows and conceives a thing, its existence follows. In us, power belongs to the moving faculty, not to the faculty that knows. God's power is not a mere capacity that may or may not be used; His action follows from will alone, without needing to consider whether He wills or does not will. His power is not like ours: our power is only a capacity, while His is fully active. Otherwise, He would contain unrealized possibility, which is impossible. And if His power were not identical with His will and knowledge, His attributes would multiply. So His power and will both return to His knowledge. Our will follows a purpose; God's only purpose is His own essence.

Avicenna also says that when things come from God's essence without an aim beyond Himself, their coming is His approval; He does not create them and only afterward approve them. God cannot have power as mere possibility. When He acts, He wills; when He does not act, it is because He does not will. His power, as such, is not about a possible choice between the two.

Wisdom means knowing the Necessary Being, the First, as He is. No created intellect knows Him as He knows Himself; He is truly wise. Philosophers also use “wisdom” to mean complete knowledge and perfect action. In understanding, complete knowledge means defining a thing if it has a definition, and knowing it through its causes if it has causes. A thing without a cause is known through itself. God, whose existence depends on nothing, cannot be defined through anything else and is known through Himself: He needs nothing else in order to be understood and has no cause.

Wisdom also means acting with perfect order. A perfect act gives each thing everything it needs to exist and continue existing, as far as it can. If its possibility lies in matter, this means giving it what its matter is ready to receive. If its possibility does not lie in matter, as with the separate intellects, it receives what its own nature allows. Different degrees of possibility explain why beings differ in their perfection and shortcomings. If possibility differs by kind, the beings differ by kind; if it differs among individuals, their degrees of completeness differ. Absolute perfection is existence without possibility, being without nonbeing, action without potential, and truth without falsehood. Everything that comes after the First is less complete, because everything other than Him is possible in itself. The degrees among later kinds and individuals follow from their different capacities. Each separate intellect is more complete than the one below it; together they are more complete than material things; and the heavens are more complete than the lower world of the elements. “More complete” here means prior in its own existence, such that the next being cannot exist without it.

These degrees of possibility also explain the presence of evil. Evil is a kind of absence, just as good is existence. The more possibility and potentiality a thing has, the more it can lack what would make it complete. That is the end of Avicenna's discussion.

Al-Tusi, one of the most careful Imami scholars, examines this question in The Refutation of the Book of Conclusions. He quotes the Ashʿarite author of The Book of Conclusions: “God must not act for an aim, contrary to the Muʿtazilites and most jurists. Anyone who acts for an aim gains some perfection through that act; one who is completed by something else is incomplete in himself. And any proposed aim is possible, so God could bring it about directly. Using an action as a means would then be pointless. We cannot say that the aim is impossible to achieve without that means, because the only suitable aim is to bring pleasure to the servant, and God can do that without any means.”

The opposing side argues that an act with no aim is pointless, and that a wise agent cannot act pointlessly. The response is: if “pointless” means only “without an aim,” this argument simply repeats itself. If it means something else, that meaning must be explained.

Al-Tusi then clarifies the Muʿtazilite view. They say that a wise agent always acts for a purpose that motivates the action; otherwise, one option would be chosen without a reason. Jurists say, for example, that the law of retaliation is meant to deter people from murder. Later jurists use this aim when deciding what the law permits or forbids in cases where scripture gives no explicit ruling. Some who affirm aims say that incomplete things are guided toward their perfection. Some perfections cannot be reached without this process, just as a body cannot move from one place to another without being moved; the movement itself serves its aim. So some aims cannot be reached without the particular actions that lead to them. It is not true in every case that God can provide the benefit directly: a person cannot receive the reward for work without doing the work.

Nor is every action without a further purpose pointless. It is pointless only when it is the kind of action that a choosing agent would normally perform for a purpose, but performs for no reason at all. The claim that any agent who acts for an aim is perfected by that aim borrows a rule from the philosophers and applies it incorrectly. Philosophers do not deny that things are guided toward their perfections. If they did, the study of the body's organs, nature, astronomy, and every other branch of natural philosophy would be pointless, and final causes would have no place. They say instead that things come from their source in the best way possible. God does not first create them incomplete and then complete them through a second act. He creates them with an inbuilt longing toward their perfection, without later needing to make a separate effort to complete them.

The Sunnis, meanwhile, say that God does whatever He wills, and that His actions cannot be judged good or bad. On this view, many incomplete beings are brought to an end before they reach their perfection, and many things in motion are moved away from the ends toward which their movement tends. God is not asked why or how He acts. That is the end of al-Tusi's argument.

The disagreement between philosophers and Ashʿarites is about whether things have causes and aims. Philosophers say every action and movement has a cause and an aim. The Ashʿarites deny cause and effect and deny that any agent—including God—must act because of a reason or motive. They define power in this way so they can say that God may choose either option without any reason favoring it. This view, as it is usually presented, is far from wisdom and knowledge. Perhaps the earliest Ashʿarite teachers meant only to deny that God acts for a further aim beyond Himself.

The disagreement between philosophers and the Muʿtazilites is narrower: does God's action as a whole have an aim beyond His own essence? Philosophers say it does not. God does not act in order to give a benefit, reward, or other good to someone else. Yet these aims and benefits follow from His actions. The Muʿtazilites say that the overall aim of His action is a benefit that returns to His servants. As for particular actions, each has a cause and aim for the agent; the agent gains a perfection through that action, either in time, as in agents in the natural world, or in a way not bound by time, as in beings above nature.

As we explained earlier, an action’s ultimate goal is also, in its full reality, what sets the agent’s action in motion. It is the first source behind the action: it brings it into being. It is also the aim when the agent has it in view. These are one thing in reality but differ in how we consider them. In the same way, the benefit that follows from an action and the end toward which it moves are one thing in reality, though we describe them differently. The goodness and completeness that the action brings about are its benefit when we see what follows from it, and its aim when we see what the action is directed toward.

A choosing agent's actions may have aims and benefits that follow one another in a chain, until they reach the final aim. That final aim is where the chain begins and ends. In God's action, all four—the goal, benefit, end, and aim—are one: His own essence. They all return to His perfect knowledge of the good order and His true will to bring about good in itself.

The greater world—the complete human being—is brought about by God, and God is its beginning and end. Each part of the order of existence has its own nearby aim and its own nearby cause, just as each part of a person's body has a nearby cause and function. In the human body, the soul is the cause and aim of the whole person. Each particular act of the body's organs has a particular power of the soul behind it—attraction, expulsion, nourishment, growth, reproduction, and many others. Their actions all return to the soul, outwardly and inwardly, as their source and end.

A created agent, because its own being is incomplete, acts for something beyond itself that completes it. God, whose essence is complete—indeed, beyond complete—has no goal or aim beyond Himself. This does not mean that His action has no aim at all: His aim is His sacred essence. Philosophers deny only that God's action as a whole has a final aim other than Himself. They call Him the aim of all aims, the end of all desires and longings, because He is the cause of causes. They do not deny that other, nearer aims and perfections follow from His actions. This differs from the Ashʿarite view, which closes the door on all explanations by causes, and the Muʿtazilite view, which gives God's action as a whole an aim beyond Himself. Both views miss the truth, which preserves the oneness of existence as the knowers of God have understood it.

We have already proved this from the point of view of God as the source and agent of existence. Here we prove it from the point of view of God as its final end. The perfection of each thing is itself, and the completion of that perfection is another perfection, continuing through the levels of being until all reach the highest perfection and complete existence. This avoids an endless chain or a circle. “Everything perishes except His face.” In this way we understand the great resurrection and the words, “Whose is the kingdom today? God's, the One, the All-Conquering.” We also understand what the people of direct insight call passing away into God and abiding in Him, and what Porphyry calls the union of the knower and the object of knowledge. The Prophet—peace be upon him—said: “I have a time with God in which no near angel or messenger prophet can share.”
Chapter 10 — God's wisdom, care, guidance, and generosity

You have learned that wisdom is the best knowledge of what is known and the most exact action in what is made. The Necessary Being knows everything through Himself, its causes and sources, and brings about the most complete order for a true end that follows from His own essence. In this sense, He is wise in His knowledge and perfect in His making and action. He is perfectly wise.

As we have seen, this very knowledge causes things to exist and is His will to bring them into existence. He does not look to anything lower than Himself as the aim of creation, nor to an end that does not belong to His essence. This is what God's care for the order of things means. Guidance is the movement by which a thing is led to a second perfection, one it does not need simply in order to exist or continue existing. God gives every thing the perfection it needs to exist and endure, and also gives it a further perfection beyond that. The Qur'an points to this when it says: “Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form, then guided it.” Creation gives the first perfection; guidance gives the second. God also says: “He created me, and He guides me.”

Generosity means giving good without receiving anything in return. Giving can take two forms: exchange and generosity. In an exchange, you give something and receive something back. The return may be a material thing, a good reputation, joy, a prayer, a new perfection, or freedom from a flaw. In short, if the giver wants something that can be gained only by giving, the act is really an exchange—even if most people use that word only when material things are traded. Those who think clearly know that true generosity has no return and no aim. Any act done for a benefit or purpose is an exchange. Only God, who depends on nothing, acts without seeking anything beyond Himself. Only He is generous in the fullest sense; every other act of generosity comes from Him.
Chapter 11 — His will extends to all actions
This is one of the subtle and difficult questions, and few people have found their way to its heart. Opinions differ, schools of thought divide, and people’s minds are left confused.

One group, including the Muʿtazilites and those who follow them, says that God created human beings and gave them the power to act, then left the choice to them. On this view, people create their actions independently, according to their own wishes and abilities. God wants them to believe and obey, and dislikes their disbelief and disobedience. They say this view explains the purpose of commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and threat of punishment, and how God is free of blame for creating and willing shameful acts and evils. But they overlook the partners they have, in effect, assigned to God.

The view that every person creates their own actions independently is even more extreme than the claim that idols or the stars intercede with God. It also means that what the King of kings wants may fail to happen in His own kingdom, while what He dislikes may still happen there. That would be a serious flaw in His rule and dominion. Exalted is God above such a thing.

Another group, including the Ashʿarites and their followers, says that everything that comes into existence does so directly by God’s will. This includes both independent beings and qualities that depend on other things, such as people’s actions, wishes, desires, movements, obedience, and disobedience. They say that God wills whatever happens and does not will what does not happen. As the familiar saying goes, everything that occurs in the world is by God’s decree and measure. The Prophet is also reported to have said, “What God wills happens, and what He does not will does not happen.” No one creates or affects anything in existence but God. He does what He wills and judges as He chooses; no cause governs His actions, and nothing can turn back His decree. “He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.” Reason, they say, has no standing to call God’s actions good or bad: everything He does is good because it comes from Him. The causes we observe—the heavens, stars, and their positions, or people and animals acting and moving—are connected to events only in appearance, not in reality. They are not truly causes and do not contribute to anything’s existence. God’s custom is simply to create a cause first and then create its effect afterward. In truth, the effects come from Him directly. They say this protects God’s power from any shortcoming or need to use something else as a means. The two groups have argued against one another, citing conflicting arguments and even verses of the Qur'an and reports from the Prophet, whose surface meanings seem to point in different directions.

A third group, the philosophers and the most learned among our Imāmī scholars, says that things differ in how they can receive existence. Some can exist only after another thing exists, as a quality cannot exist without a substance. God’s power is perfect: He gives existence to possible things in an ordered sequence, according to their different capacities. Some things come from Him without an intermediate cause; others come through one cause or many. They enter existence only after the things that cause them are already there. God is the cause of causes, with no cause before Him. This does not show a limit in His power. The limit is in what can receive existence. Nor is there any need or dependence in this: the intermediate cause also comes from Him, so God depends on no one in bringing anything into existence.

There is no doubt that the world comes from a source that is perfect in goodness and generosity, and that what comes from Him must follow the finest order. What comes from Him is either pure good, like the angels and beings like them, or something in which good outweighs evil, like jinn and human beings. Good comes from God directly, while the evils that accompany it come only indirectly. In this sense, people have said that God wills the disbelief and sins people commit, but does not approve of them. Consider someone bitten by a snake whose life can be saved only by cutting off a finger. The person chooses the amputation in order to save their life. They want the life-saving result and approve of it; they choose the amputation, but do not approve of it in itself. This is the subtle distinction. This view is better than the first two, free of their worst problems, and closer to the truth for anyone who sees what lies beneath appearances. It is a middle way between compulsion and complete independence: the best course is the middle one.

A fourth group—the people firmly grounded in knowledge, the people of God—says that although beings differ in their essences, qualities, actions, and nearness to or distance from the First Reality, they are all gathered within one divine reality that contains every level and truth. This does not mean that God is a composite made up of all things. God is far above multiplicity and composition. It means that this divine reality, though utterly simple and one, sends its light throughout the heavens and the earth. No particle in the world of existence lies outside the encompassing power of the Light of lights. “He watches over every soul and what it has earned.” He is with everything, but not by being beside it; He is beyond everything, but not by being separated from it. “He is God in heaven and God on earth.”

This subtle and noble truth was discovered through spiritual practice and direct insight. We have also established it through proof, in a way that agrees with what is seen and known directly. Just as nothing in existence falls outside God’s activity, so no action falls outside His action. This does not mean that Zayd’s action does not truly come from Zayd. It means that the very action that truly belongs to Zayd also truly belongs to God. Judgment belongs to God alone; there is no power or strength except through God, the Most High, the Most Great. Every power is His power. In all His greatness and exaltedness, He takes on the actions of things; and in all His transcendence, He is present in every earth and heaven, as the Qur'an says: “He is with you wherever you are.”

Once this is understood, it becomes clear that actions and existence can truly be attributed to a human being, just as hearing, sight, and the other senses, their powers, actions, and responses can truly be attributed to us. Zayd’s existence is real and belongs to Zayd, not merely in a figure of speech; at the same time, it is one of the ways the First Reality is present in the world. The same is true of Zayd’s knowledge, will, movement, stillness, and everything else he does. These truly belong to him, and at the same time they are actions of the Real in a higher and nobler way, suited to God’s oneness, without weakness, passivity, resemblance, or contact with bodies and impurities. Exalted is He above all that.

Transcendence belongs to God’s oneness, in which everything else is overcome: He is the One who prevails, and there is no other beside Him. Resemblance belongs to the many levels of created things and their dependence on Him. All praise returns to His one reality, while the many acts of praise and worship belong to the created order.

God gives existence to everything that exists. Existence is pure good, and existence is what He gives. Evil and nonexistence are not created; neither are essences that have never received existence. A dog’s body may be impure, but the existence it receives from God is pure. A person may be impure in essence because of what they are, but not in the existence God gives them, which is pure at its source. Existence becomes mixed with absence and darkness as it moves farther from the source of generosity and light. Sunlight falling on filth does not lose its brightness or become foul-smelling; it only seems so because it falls on something foul. In the same way, existence, simply as existence and as an effect of existence, is good and beautiful. Evil and ugliness come from its incompleteness, or from its conflict with another good. Both come down to some kind of absence, and absence is not created. All praise belongs to God, the Most High, the Most Great.

This is the heart of the fourth view. Understanding the soul and its powers makes it easier to grasp: every action of the senses and of the animal and natural powers is an action of the soul, while still truly being an action of those powers. This fourth view is greatly fruitful and profound, if anyone can reach it. It removes the difficulties surrounding the creation of human actions and makes sense of the saying of the Imam of those who affirm God’s oneness, ʿAlī: “No compulsion and no delegation, but a matter between the two.”

This does not mean that a person’s action is made up partly of compulsion and partly of independence. Nor does it mean that the action falls outside both, or that a person is free in one respect and forced in another, or that someone is forced while appearing to choose, as some have said. Nor does it mean that people have a little freedom and a little compulsion. It means that a person is free precisely in being dependent on God, and dependent on God precisely in being free.

The saying “the best course is the middle one” has a deeper meaning here. Sometimes a middle state is a blend of two extremes, like lukewarm water: it is neither hot nor cold, though it belongs to the same range as both. This kind of middle state is still a mixture. But a middle state can also unite two qualities on a higher, simpler level, where they do not oppose or crowd one another. The heavenly sphere, as philosophers understand it, is an example: it has both heat and cold, each in a higher and simpler form than what we find in this world. In this analogy, the first view is like fire’s heat, the second like water’s cold, the third like lukewarm water, and the fourth like the state of the heavenly sphere.

You who seek a true understanding of things and hope to reach the world of holiness: do not be devoted only to saying God is unlike creation, nor only to saying He is like creation, nor settle for a confused mixture of both. Hold the belief of those who dwell in the sanctuaries of the realm of power. They are beyond both likeness and negation, and beyond mixing opposites. They belong to the divine unity that gathers all things. God is exalted in His nearness and near in His exaltedness. His mercy encompasses everything. No being, action, affair, will, or wish lies outside Him. That is why He says, “Every day He is at work,” and, “There is no private conversation among three where He is not the fourth, nor among five where He is not the sixth.” This also reveals the meaning of, “You did not throw when you threw, but God threw.” The statement both denies and affirms the act from the same point of view. Likewise, “Fight them; God will punish them by your hands” attributes the killing to the people and the punishment to God, though the punishment there is the very act of killing.
This is what I have to say about the creation of human actions, a question that has confused many minds. God is the source of right guidance and understanding.

One example can make this easier to understand: read the book of the human soul. It is a shorter version of the great book of the world, written by the All-Merciful, who has taken mercy upon Himself and written faith in your hearts. Reflect on the soul and on the actions of its powers. Then you will see that actions coming from human beings are also, in the very same reality, actions of God—not as the determinists say, not as those who claim complete human independence say, and not as the philosophers’ usual account has it. Consider the senses and powers of the human soul: God made them an example of His own essence, attributes, and actions. “And in yourselves—will you not see?” The Messenger of God also said, “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”

The truth, seen with care, is that every action of a sense or power, insofar as it is the action of that power, is also the action of the soul. Seeing is certainly the action of sight, since sight either brings the visible image before us or receives it. Hearing is the action of hearing, since it either brings the sound into awareness or receives it. Neither can happen without bodily change. Yet each is also the action of the soul, which is truly the one that hears and sees. It is not enough to say, as the standard philosophical account does, that the soul merely uses its powers, as someone might hire a writer or painter. Hiring a craftsman does not make the employer the craftsman: someone who hires a builder need not be a builder, and someone who hires a writer need not be a writer. So merely using sight or hearing would not make the soul seeing or hearing.

But if we look within, we know that the soul itself is the one that perceives in every act of sense and awareness, and that it is the one that moves in every animal or natural movement attributed to our powers. We will explain later how the soul itself is the power of sight in the eye, hearing in the ear, grasping in the hand, and walking in the foot. Through it, the eye sees, the ear hears, the hand grasps, and the foot walks. This recalls the sacred saying: “I am his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, and his hand by which he grasps.”

Though the soul is one and separate from the body and its powers, no part of the body—high or low, subtle or dense—is outside it. Nor are the perceiving and moving powers, whether animal or natural, separate in their reality from the soul. The soul’s oneness is a different kind of oneness, known by those who see directly. It is a shadow of divine being: one encompassing reality that gathers all the identities of the powers, senses, and organs. When the soul’s complete reality appears, their separate identities fade into it, and their individual existence gives way to its one existence.

At death, which is the lesser resurrection of every being in the small world of the human body, these powers fade in their scattered bodily forms. At the second blowing of the trumpet, they take on another life, a single and gathered existence through the soul. Then they rise and look on. The land of the body in the next life shines with the soul’s light, just as the whole world will shine in the great resurrection. The soul encompasses and rules its powers; they begin from it and return to it. The soul’s rising begins with God and ends with God. So it is with all beings: “From Him they begin, and to Him they return. Truly, all affairs return to God.”
Chapter 12 — Answering the remaining objections to eternal will, and some objections to created will

One objection is that if God’s will is as the philosophers and careful Muslim thinkers describe it—identical with His essence and with the motive behind His actions, namely, His knowledge of the most complete order—then the world must be eternal and His will must fail to happen at the time He wills it. We have answered this in our discussions of the coming-to-be of bodies and physical natures, and of how events are connected to the divine reality.

Another objection appeals to God’s words, “He is not questioned about what He does.” If any of His actions were directed toward a goal or motive beyond Himself, someone might reasonably ask why He acted as He did. Why, then, do the Qur'an and the reports forbid this question? The answer is that they do not deny that God’s actions have causes or aims, as the Ashʿarites and their followers suppose. Rather, as we have already explained, they deny that God’s action as a whole has some final aim beyond Himself. Particular actions may still have nearer and intermediate aims.

For example, the broad back teeth are shaped to help us chew well. Good chewing serves the first stage of digestion, which serves the next stage, which in turn helps nourish the body in a way suited to its nature. That supports a healthy bodily balance, which allows the soul to reach its perfection. The soul’s perfection leads to the intellect’s development, first as a capacity and then in full, and finally to the active intellect. The ultimate aim is God, exalted above all. The same pattern appears in learning: grammar and language help us learn logic, which serves the theoretical sciences that are not merely tools. Taken together, those sciences are their own final aim, since they are the end of the sciences that serve them. But considered separately, some can be the aim of others: the study of nature, motion, and generation and decay leads to the questions of metaphysics.

Metaphysics, in turn, leads to the study of immaterial beings and divine things, and from there to the knowledge of God’s oneness, His attributes, and the origin and return of all things. As knowledge, this has its own end; as a way of being, its end is nearness to God. Its aim is to pass away into divine oneness and then abide after that passing. It has no further aim: it is the aim of all aims and the highest of all states.

So there is no further “why?” behind God’s action as a whole, or behind the last act in the order. But the particular, nearer, and intermediate actions do have aims and explanations, arranged in a chain that leads to the One who is the aim of every aim and the end of every longing, through His own true and utterly one essence.

Another objection says that if everything happens by God’s will and decree, then reason and religious law require us to approve of every decree. A sacred report says: “Whoever is not content with My decree, does not endure My trial with patience, and is not grateful for My gifts, let that person leave My earth and heaven and seek another lord.” Yet approving disbelief and wrongdoing is itself disbelief and wrongdoing. Reports from the Imams say that approving disbelief is disbelief, and the Qur'an says that God does not approve disbelief for His servants.

Al-Ghazālī and others, including Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, answer that disbelief is what God decrees, not the decree itself. It is the object of the decree, not the decree; so we approve the decree, not what is decreed. Some Sufis, including the author of ʿAwārif al-maʿārif and Jalāl al-Dīn Rumi, accepted this answer. But skilled scholars, among them Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi in his Naqd al-Muḥaṣṣal, rejected it. He says that when someone says, “I am content with God’s decree,” they do not mean that they approve one of God’s attributes. They mean that they approve what that attribute brings about—what is decreed.

The correct answer, according to him, is that approving something because it is God’s decree is obedience, not disbelief; it is disbelief only when approved for some other reason. Our honored teacher says that the distinction between decree and what is decreed does not solve the problem: considering something as decreed is just another way of considering the decree, while considering it apart from that relation is not considering it as decreed. The sound answer is that we must approve the decree as decree, and what is decreed as decreed. Disbelief, however, is not decreed in itself or directly. It is decreed only indirectly, as something that follows from many goods. We approve it only in that respect, not because it is disbelief. Disbelief lies in approving disbelief as disbelief, rather than accepting something because it is bound up with the many goods of the order of existence.

I say that “decree,” like “judgment,” can mean the affirmative or negative relation expressed in a judgment. That is a relation, and what is decreed is its object. Or “decree” can mean the intelligible image that includes such a relation. The same distinction applies to knowledge, power, will, and similar terms. On the first meaning, if the decree itself is approved, then what is decreed must be approved too, because a relation follows its object. If someone says that a judge has issued an evil or unjust judgment, they mean the object of the judgment. There is no sense in saying that the judgment is good while what it judges is evil.

On the second meaning, God’s decree is the existence of all the things in this lower world as they exist in His knowledge: in a sacred, intellectual, and divine form, free of limitation, evil, nonexistence, possibility, and darkness. Every being in this world has a corresponding reality in that divine world: a positive reality that causes it and gives rise to it. There it is pure good, with no evil mixed in. The world of command is entirely good; evil is found only in the world of creation, where existence is mixed with absence and darkness. That is why the Qur'an says, “I seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak from the evil of what He has created,” placing evil on the side of created things.

With this distinction, the claim that we should approve God’s decree but not necessarily everything decreed makes sense. But Tusi’s point—that “I am content with God’s decree” does not mean that one approves an attribute of God—still needs an answer. God’s decree is not a quality added to Him. It is the source and reality of beings themselves. Nor do we accept that being content with God’s decree means only being content with what He knew beforehand.

There is also a problem with the claim that approving disbelief as God’s decree is obedience, not disbelief. Since God’s knowledge is active, every positive aspect of anything in this world is also the very aspect by which it is known to Him. Just as God and His knowledge of things are one without any difference in His essence or even in how we consider Him, so too a thing’s existence in itself and its being known to Him are one reality, with no difference between them.

Here is an example that may make the point clearer. If you picture someone as a disbeliever or imagine their face as black, that image does not make you a disbeliever or blacken the face of your heart. The image of disbelief in the mind is not blameworthy disbelief, and the image of blackness in the mind is not the same blackness found outside it. Keep that distinction firmly in mind, and do not stumble over it.

The source of an evil or ugly thing in the world of bodies need not itself be evil or flawed. Those who know the divine names explain that God’s majestic and overpowering names—such as the Avenger, the Compeller, and the All-Conquering—are sources of evils and harmful things, including disbelievers, devils, wrongdoers, and the levels of Hell and its inhabitants. His gentle and beautiful names—such as the All-Merciful, the Compassionate, the Kind, and the Subtle—are sources of good things, including the prophets, saints, believers, and the levels of Paradise and its inhabitants. They even say that Satan was created through the name “the Misleader,” citing his words, “Because You led me astray,” and “Because You made me err.” What clashes in the world of separation, evil, and conflict fits together in the world of unity and good.

Another objection says that if God knows a human action and His will and decree apply to it, then the action must necessarily occur. If He does not know it and His will and decree do not apply to it, then it cannot occur. How, then, can a person have power over their own action?

The objection can be answered by showing that the same problem applies to God’s will for events that come into being in time, especially if His will is said to change over time. But there is also a direct answer. Al-Rāzī, in al-Muḥaṣṣal, and those who follow him say that this objection applies to everyone; God is not questioned about what He does. We have already considered this response. In his critique, Tusi says: if this argument disproved human power and choice, it would also disprove God’s power and choice, since He knew from eternity what He would do in the future. His action in the future must be either necessary or impossible. He replies that knowledge follows what is known, so it does not make the known action necessary or impossible.

Taken at face value, this answer is not sound. Knowledge follows its object only when the knowledge is passive and comes into being after the thing known. God’s decree, however, is active knowledge: it is the cause of things’ existence, not something that follows them. Perhaps Tusi offered this answer on behalf of the Muʿtazilites, who say that things had a reality from eternity in their own right.

The right answer is that although God’s knowledge causes a human action to exist, it causes that action to occur through the person’s power and choice, which come before the action and are among its causes. Necessity through choice does not cancel choice; it is what makes the action a chosen one. God’s essence is the active cause of everything that exists, and of its necessity. This does not remove the role of intermediate causes and conditions or the order connecting causes to effects. The same is true of God’s complete knowledge of everything, which is His essence in the case of simple knowledge, or follows from His essence in the case of detailed knowledge.

It is remarkable that this great debater sometimes let the truth show through, even though elsewhere he insisted on defending the Ashʿarite denial of cause and effect. In al-Mabāḥith al-mashriqiyya, he writes that, once examined carefully, the question of whether the world is eternal or created and the question of compulsion or free choice rest on the same point: whenever an agent’s power is only possible, its action cannot follow unless something else makes it happen. This is the key premise in both debates.

Since God’s power cannot be made necessary by anything separate from Him, it must be necessary through His own essence. And when His power is necessary through Himself, His action is eternal. A human being’s power, by contrast, cannot be necessary through the person’s own essence, since neither the person nor their power to act exists eternally. So human action must depend on God. It follows that human actions occur by God’s decree and measure.

Someone might object: if everything happens by God’s decree, what is the point of commands, prohibitions, reward, and punishment? And if God’s decree makes an action necessary or impossible, then our power cannot apply to it, since power cannot apply to what is necessary or impossible. Yet we know directly that we can act. This seems to disprove the account.

He answers that commands and prohibitions also occur by decree. Reward and punishment follow from actions that occur by decree, just as bad food causes bodily illness, and false beliefs and wrong actions cause illness in the soul. The same is true of reward. As for power, an action’s being necessary does not prevent it from being something we can do. The action’s necessity follows from the necessity of the power; an effect does not cancel its cause. An action is not within our power only when it is necessary for some reason other than our power.

He supports this by pointing out that people who hold this view say God must give reward and compensate people for suffering in the next life. If He failed to do what is required, that would imply either ignorance or need, both of which are impossible for God. So it is impossible for Him not to give reward and compensation; therefore, giving them is necessary. Yet this action is still within His power. So the kind of necessity described here does not prevent an action from being within the agent’s power.

This is closer to the truth than his other writings. The argument in al-Muḥaṣṣal that all acts of will must end in a necessary act of will, to avoid an infinite chain, does not reach this level. In his critique, Tusi says that before an action is linked to God’s decree, it either comes about without an intermediary or through one. The first does not show that all acts of will end in God’s will; the second does not rule out choice, since a chosen action is one that comes through power and will, whether these come from God directly or through another cause. Therefore, some actions occur by God’s decree precisely through the agent’s choice.

I say that there is a real difference between saying that nothing exists unless God is its cause, and saying that God alone is the cause of anything that exists. The first is true; the second is not. As we explained in the previous chapter, the very respect in which an action is attributed to a human being is also the respect in which it is attributed to God. The action comes from the person in the very respect in which it comes from God.

This noble question—the oneness of actions—is among the greatest questions in divine philosophy. Though nearly all philosophers claim to have understood it, no one has reached it, as far as I can tell from reading their works, except someone to whom it has been revealed through certain proof and holy light. Tusi reports in his commentary on the Ishārāt that all philosophers agree that existence as a whole is caused by God. But who among those we know, whose books and words we have examined, has truly seen the oneness of God’s essence?

Another objection says that human will comes from outside us through causes that ultimately go back to God’s eternal will. So our will must occur whether we want it or not; God’s necessary will forces us into it. “You do not will unless God wills.” How can our actions be by our will if our will is not itself willed by us? If it were, there would be an endless chain of wills.

The answer is that a person is a willing agent when their action follows their will, not when their will itself follows another will. Otherwise, a person’s will could not be identical with their own self. A person has power when, if they will to act, they can act, and if they do not will to act, they do not act—not when they can will their own will. One could add that willing to will resembles knowing that one knows or the existence of existence: the mind can form these ideas repeatedly, without end, but the chain stops when the mind stops considering them. There is no chain of causes in the world outside the mind.

Our honored teacher offers another answer. He says that when a chain of causes leads a person to picture an action and believe it to be good, desire for it arises. When that desire grows strong and settled, the will takes shape and sets the limbs and organs in motion. This will is one general state of longing in the soul. If we attend to the action itself, it is desire and will for that action. If instead we focus on the act of willing, the same state is desire and will for the act of willing. The same is true if we focus on willing the will, or on any further level the mind can consider in detail. Each detailed act of will is an act of will, but all are contained in that one general state of longing. Their order in thought does not prevent them from being one in the soul’s single felt state. This kind of division applies only to extended quantities and things that stretch through space. A distance, for example, cannot be divided into parts that are inherently earlier and later; its parts are earlier or later only by where they lie.
